author: William Saville
reader_character: Jasper — adult first-person protagonist, externally they/them
title: The Terms of Us
subtitle: The Lanternweald — expansion pass three
content:
Severus did not shout when I told him I had forgotten dinner.

He looked at the clock, then at the covered plates, and said, "I see."

That was worse.

The plates were on the kitchen table at Spinner's End, protected by a warming charm that had kept the food from going cold. Severus had even put out the good tea service. I had promised him a quiet evening after the committee meeting. Instead, I'd stayed at Riverstone Terrace while Katara's clinic volunteers were preparing supplies for the South.

I had sent a note.

The note had been delivered after dinner was supposed to begin.

"I'm sorry," I said.

He folded his napkin carefully.

"Forgetting is inconvenient. Informing me after the appointed hour is discourteous."

"You're right."

"Of course I am."

I wanted to argue that the work had been urgent. It had been. I wanted to explain that Katara's departure was emotional for everyone involved. It was. None of those facts had made the note arrive on time.

"I should have told you the moment I realized I couldn't make it," I said. "I didn't."

Severus looked at me for several seconds.

"Thank you."

He did not say he forgave me. He did not have to.

I took off my coat and hung it beside his. The hall was damp from rain, and the lamps burned with the familiar yellow light that made the chipped wallpaper look almost warm.

"Would you like me to leave?" I asked.

He seemed genuinely surprised.

"No. I would like you to stop standing in the doorway as though I intend to expel you."

That was enough of an invitation.

I sat across from him.

We ate dinner together, but we didn't pretend the issue had gone away. He asked about the supplies. I told him what I could without sharing the clinic's private medical information. He offered a correction to the preservation method for one herb, and I wrote it down.

Then he set his fork aside.

"Are our arrangements still what you want?"

I looked up.

"Which arrangements?"

"Your relationships. My place among them."

I had known the question would come eventually. I was only surprised he had chosen to ask it so plainly.

"Yes," I said. "I'm ethically non-monogamous, and I still prefer polyamory. I care about you, and I care about other people. None of that has changed."

He watched my face.

"I am not asking you to change it."

"Then what are you asking?"

He looked down at his hands.

"Whether I have mistaken my willingness to be discreet for a willingness to be forgotten."

It hurt to hear, because it was precise.

"I don't want you to feel forgotten."

"That was not my question."

I took a breath.

"No. You haven't mistaken anything. I assumed you'd understand because you're private. That's unfair."

He nodded once.

Severus was not a person who wanted grand declarations in crowded rooms. He did not want to attend every feast or make the names of my partners part of a public inventory. He did want to know when I was coming home. He wanted the freedom to decline gatherings without being interpreted as jealous or ashamed. He wanted me to ask rather than presume that a missed evening could be absorbed without consequence.

I took out my notebook.

He raised an eyebrow.

"Must everything become documentation?"

"Only the things I keep getting wrong."

"An extensive volume."

I gave him a look.

He almost smiled.

We made a list, though it was more a conversation than a contract.

He wanted advance notice when plans changed, unless a genuine emergency made it impossible. I wanted him to tell me when he needed reassurance instead of delivering increasingly elegant insults until I guessed correctly. He wanted privacy around details of my other relationships, not because he disapproved but because he considered intimate lives a poor subject for casual conversation. I wanted him to understand that being discreet about us didn't mean hiding that I cared for him.

"Are we allowed to be seen together?" I asked.

He looked insulted.

"Certainly."

"At a public tea tasting?"

"Do not push your luck."

I laughed.

He rolled his eyes and, because he knew me, offered his hand across the table.

I took it.

"And what of my time?" he asked.

"What about it?"

"You have spent a considerable amount of energy arranging yourself around everyone else's needs. What do you require?"

I had been prepared for his hurt. I had not prepared for his concern.

"I need to be able to say no," I admitted. "Even to people I love. I need writing time. Quiet time. And I need to know that if I make a mistake, we can talk about it without treating the entire relationship as a failure."

Severus squeezed my fingers.

"An eminently sensible set of demands."

"Really?"

"Do not sound so surprised. You are occasionally sensible."

"Should I note the date?"

"Please don't."

The rain grew heavier outside. It tapped the window in uneven rhythms, and the candle flame bent every time the old house shifted.

Severus stood to clear the plates. I helped without asking him to accept a performance of penitence. We washed the dishes and put the good cups away. Small ordinary tasks had a way of letting an argument settle into its proper size.

In the hallway, he stopped me.

"Jasper."

"Yes?"

"I had been afraid that asking for more of your attention would mean asking you to love someone else less."

I went still.

"That isn't how it works," I said. "We can discuss time and boundaries without comparing people as if they're numbers on a scale."

"I know that in theory."

"And in practice?"

He considered the question.

"In practice, I am learning."

I stepped closer.

"Me too."

He lifted a hand to my face. There was hesitation in the movement, not because he doubted I cared, but because he understood the value of asking even after a long history together.

"May I kiss you?"

"Yes."

His lips met mine, slow at first, then warmer when I rested a hand against his chest. I could feel his heart beneath the fabric, steady and human and nothing like the frightening legend other people had made of him.

When we parted, he kept his hand against my cheek.

"Tomorrow," he said, "I would like breakfast."

"With me?"

"An appalling deduction."

"I can be here."

"If that changes, tell me before the porridge is ruined."

I laughed against his shoulder.

We spent the rest of the evening together, with the rain closing the world to one small kitchen and one open doorway. No one else had to disappear for that moment to matter.

The next morning I arrived when I said I would.

Severus had laid out two bowls.

There was no celebration. No dramatic proof that we'd solved ethical non-monogamy once and for all.

We ate breakfast, and when I left for Moonroot Archive, I told him when I expected to return.

That was the beginning of keeping the terms of us.
